tytul: Fennel seeds and leaves dried by the herb method
wstep: This card describes how to dry fennel seeds and leaves in paper bags or in a food dehydrator, using the NCHFP method for herbs; NCHFP does not name fennel.

akapity: Herbs (leaves, flowers or seeds) are dried by exposing them to warm, dry air in a well-ventilated place until the moisture evaporates.
After harvest, do not leave the herbs in the sun or unattended, and avoid bruising the leaves.
Rinse the herbs in cool water, gently shake off excess water and discard bruised, soiled or damaged leaves and stems.
Without a dehydrator, hang herbs with seeds in paper bags with holes in the sides, a small bunch per bag (large bunches go mouldy), where air currents circulate through the bag.
Do not dry herbs in the sun: they can lose flavour and colour.
In a dehydrator, dry herbs at 95–115 °F (about 35–46 °C) in a single layer on the trays; in humid areas up to 125 °F (about 52 °C) may be needed, and drying takes 1–4 hours.
Do not use trays or screens made of galvanized mesh; also avoid copper and aluminium mesh.
The leaves are dry when they crumble and the stems break when bent; leaves ready for packing are crisp and crumble easily between your fingers.
Remove husks from the dried seeds by rubbing them between your hands and blowing away the chaff.
Pack only completely cooled dried food: warm dried food sweats, and that moisture can be enough for mould to grow.
Dried food is susceptible to insects and moisture reabsorption, so once completely cool, pack it at once into clean, dry insect-proof containers, as tightly as possible without crushing.
Store dried food in clean, dry canning jars, plastic freezer containers with tight-fitting lids or plastic freezer bags.
Packaging must be food grade: do not use trash bags or plastic or fibreboard containers that previously held non-food items.
Pack amounts that can be used at one time: each opening exposes the dried food to air and moisture, which lowers quality and can lead to spoilage.
Vacuum packaging is not a preservation method by itself: removing oxygen increases the risk of botulism, and a product that needs refrigeration still needs it.
Store dried food in a cool, dry, dark place.
Airtight containers and a cool, dry, dark place protect the colour and fragrance of the herbs.
Dried herbs are usually 3–4 times stronger than fresh; use 1/4–1/3 of the amount of fresh herbs in a recipe.
Check dried food often (glass shows condensation); if it has taken up moisture but is not spoiled, use it at once or dry it again and repack it.
Throw away mouldy dried food; also throw away any that smells off.
